title: Binary tree
learningGoals: insert into a binary search tree
print a tree in sorted order
search a tree and find its height

youtube.title: C++ Binary Search Tree: Insert, Search, Traverse | C++ Programming EP 86
youtube.description: In this episode you will insert into a binary search tree, print a tree in sorted order and search a tree and find its height, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Binary tree · 1:17 Insert and print in order · 2:35 The tree · 3:16 Second program · 4:53 Recap · 5:23 Bug of the Day · 6:15 Challenge · 6:41 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we build a tree. Each node has two children. Small numbers go left, and big numbers go right.

scenes.onScreen: "Binary tree": numbered lines (1. Each node has a left and a right child; 2. Smaller keys go left; 3. Inorder traversal prints sorted keys) and an analogy card: a family tree where small numbers go left and big numbers go right
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A binary search tree keeps its keys in order. For each node, every key in the left side is smaller, and every key in the right side is bigger. Recursion fits trees well. To insert, compare the key, then go left or right, and repeat. Trees are everywhere. A file system is a tree. A family tree is a tree. The set and the map in the library are trees inside. In a balanced tree, each step halves the work. For a million keys, a search takes about twenty steps. A plain tree can lean, and then it behaves like a list. Real libraries keep the tree balanced.
points: Each node has a left and a right child

analogy.title: Binary tree
analogy.body: A family tree where small numbers go left and big numbers go right

scenes.onScreen: tree.cpp: five keys are inserted and printed in sorted order
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 10] Insert returns the root of the tree after the change. [HL 11] An empty spot is the base case. We make a new node there. [HL 14] A smaller key goes into the left side. [HL 16] A bigger key goes into the right side. [HL 42] We insert five, three, eight, one and four. [HL 26] Inorder visits the left side first. [HL 27] Then it prints the node. [HL 28] Then it visits the right side. The output is one three four five eight. [HL 35] Destroy deletes the children first, and then the node. [HL 10] The insert function returns the root of the tree. [HL 11] An empty spot is where the new node goes. [HL 14] A smaller key goes to the left. [HL 16] A bigger key goes to the right. [HL 26] The in order walk visits the left side, then the node, then the right side. The output is one, three, four, five, eight.

scenes.onScreen: a tree with five, three, eight, one and four
scenes.animation: Nodes pop in one by one; edges draw on as the narrator mentions them
scenes.narration: Five is the root. Three is smaller, so it goes left. Eight is bigger, so it goes right. One goes left of three, and four goes right of three. Notice how the tree grows. Five is the first key, so it is the root. Three is smaller, so it goes left. Eight is bigger, so it goes right. Reading the tree from left to right gives a sorted list.

diagram.caption: a tree with five, three, eight, one and four

scenes.onScreen: search.cpp: the tree is searched, and its height is measured
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 23] Contains follows one path only. [HL 25] An empty spot means the key is not in the tree. [HL 27] A match means the key is in the tree. [HL 30] Otherwise it goes left or right, as insert did. Four is in the tree, so we get true. Seven is not, so we get false. [HL 33] Height is one plus the height of the taller child. [HL 37] Max picks the taller side. This tree has height three. [HL 23] The contains function asks, is the key here? [HL 27] If the key matches, the answer is true. [HL 30] Otherwise, it goes left or right, and asks again. It never looks at the other side. [HL 37] The height is one plus the taller of the two sides. For our tree, it is three.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as search dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints one three four five eight, then true, false, and three. Notice the output. Four is in the tree, seven is not, and the height is three.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A binary search tree keeps keys in order. Two. Smaller keys go left, and bigger keys go right. Three. Inorder traversal prints the keys in sorted order. Four. Recursion fits trees well. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A binary search tree keeps keys in order.
Smaller keys go left, and bigger keys go right.
Inorder traversal prints the keys in sorted order.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Printing before the left side
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The keys come out as five three one four, which is not sorted. The code prints the node before the left side. Visit left first, then print, then visit right. The place of the print line decides the order. Left first, then the node, then the right side, gives sorted output. If you print the node before the left side, you get preorder, and the numbers come out in another order.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the tree win the race? It had strong roots, and it never lost its balance.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the tree win the race? It had strong roots, and it never lost its balance.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: find the smallest key
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a function that returns the smallest key in a binary search tree. Hint: keep going left. Hint: loop while the left pointer is not null, and move to the left child each time. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: threads and mutex. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Program output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

5 3 1 4
bug.why: The order of the three lines decides the traversal. Left, node, right gives sorted order. Node first gives preorder, which is not sorted.

pun: "Why did the tree win the race? It had strong roots, and it never lost its balance."
challenge: Write a function that returns the smallest key in a binary search tree. Hint: keep going left. Hint: loop while the left pointer is not null, and move to the left child each time.
challengeAnswer: Start at the root. While the left child is not null, move to the left child. Return that key.
